old.name: Port de Cavalaire — the ancient Heraclea anchorage
old.hook: This deep, south-facing bay is generally identified as the old port of Heraclea Caccabaria, named in the Roman Antonine Itinerary — a well-sheltered anchorage screened from the Mistral, which is exactly why Greek, then Roman, then medieval traders used it. Small fishing boats (the traditional pointus) still work it, and the crews sell the morning catch on the quay. No ancient masonry survives above water; the harbour's real relic is the shelter itself.

old.name: Pardigon
old.hook: A green amphitheatre of former farmland and wetland set back behind the beach, backed by the Maures foothills and threaded by the Carrade stream — grazing, reeds and, buried under the grass, two excavated Roman villas.
old.text: A green amphitheatre of former farmland and wetland set back behind the beach, backed by the Maures foothills and threaded by the Carrade stream — grazing, reeds and, buried under the grass, two excavated Roman villas. It is the rarest thing on this coast: an undeveloped coastal plain in the middle of a summer-resort strip. It survived only after years of court fights — the Conseil d'État declared it a 'site remarquable du littoral', permanently non-buildable, which let the Conservatoire du littoral acquire it and make it inalienable in January 2011. Digs in the 1980s revealed two Roman wine estates straddling the Carrade, one on each commune. It's now being re-wilded: the dune cord rebuilt, the behind-dune wet meadows restored. Signal Made inalienable under the Conservatoire du littoral in January 2011 (declared a 'site remarquable du littoral'); Roman villas excavated in the 1980s

old.name: Église Saint-Laurent
old.hook: The parish church — and a lesson in how young the resort town is. Begun in 1910 as a modest chapel dependent on the older hill-village of Gassin, enlarged in 1932, it became a parish in its own right only in 1960. Not a medieval monument: it is the stone record of Cavalaire's early-20th-century birth as a seaside town.

old.name: Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des Méditerranées
old.hook: A ~20-hectare hillside garden (about 7 ha planted) that sets the world's Mediterranean-climate regions side by side — Chile, California, South Africa, Australia, the Canaries — tumbling down to the Baie du Figuier opposite the Golden Isles.
old.text: A ~20-hectare hillside garden (about 7 ha planted) that sets the world's Mediterranean-climate regions side by side — Chile, California, South Africa, Australia, the Canaries — tumbling down to the Baie du Figuier opposite the Golden Isles. Terroir made literal: the Var coast rebuilt as a living atlas of every dry-summer climate on earth. Begun in 1910 as the retreat of Parisian businessman Alfred Courmes (his first villa became the Hôtel de la Mer), bought in 1940 by aviation magnate Henry Potez who added an Art-Deco garden, then left to run wild for years. In 1989 the Conservatoire du Littoral rescued it and handed the redesign to Gilles Clément, the gardener-philosopher of the 'jardin en mouvement.' You learn the idea of climatic analogues — why a Cape Town protea and a Californian ceanothus thrive in the same Provençal soil. Signal Verified: created 1910 (Courmes, a Parisian businessman; his first house became the Hôtel de la Mer), Potez from 1940, saved 1989 by Conservatoire du Littoral, redesigned by Gilles Clément; ~20 ha, more than 4,000 species today — Wikipedia / Conservatoire du littoral

old_also.name: Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des Méditerranées
old_also.hook: A 20-hectare protected domain of the Conservatoire du littoral, its gardens designed by landscape architect Gilles Clément to gather the world's Mediterranean-climate floras — California, Chile, South Africa, Australia, the Canaries — around an early-20th-century villa above a private cove. In summer a guided 'sentier marin' lets you snorkel the protected Baie du Figuier. The finest single outing near Cavalaire, and a real botanical education, not a municipal flowerbed.

old.name: Espace Archéologique Municipal Aristide Fabre
old.hook: The town's small municipal archaeological room — on the ground floor of the médiathèque — tracing Cavalaire's deep past through collections, models and panels: the Iron Age oppidum of Montjean, and above all the Gallo-Roman villas of Pardigon, which made and shipped wine from this very coast. It is the honest key to the 'Heraclea Caccabaria' story — the port that Roman sailing itineraries record here — because nothing of the ancient harbour still stands above water; what survives of it is gathered, in fragments, in this one room. Rotating exhibitions supplement the permanent display.

old.name: Monument du Débarquement de Provence
old.hook: A granite twin-column memorial (by architect G. Nadal, 2nd Grand Prix de Rome) to the Allied landing of 15–16 August 1944, Operation Dragoon. Cavalaire's beach was codenamed 'Alpha'; General de Lattre's Army B came ashore here on 16 August. This — not a medieval castle — is the town's true fortification story: the German coastal defences of the so-called 'Mur de la Méditerranée' were overrun in the days that followed. Three granite blocks nearby mark the 1st DFL and US units.

old_also.name: Monument du Débarquement, Plage de Cavalaire (Alpha Beach)
old_also.hook: An open-air landing memorial on the seafront promenade, marking where the Allied invasion of southern France came ashore. Free, always open; walk it, don't queue for it.
old_also.text: An open-air landing memorial on the seafront promenade, marking where the Allied invasion of southern France came ashore. Free, always open; walk it, don't queue for it. The terroir truth locals live with: this mild holiday bay was code-named Alpha Beach. On 15 August 1944, Operation Dragoon — the 'other' D-Day that history forgets behind Normandy — put the US 3rd Infantry Division ashore right here. The following evening, around 7pm on 16 August, General Jean de Lattre's Army B (the French First Army, eventually a quarter-million men drawn from the Free French and the Army of Africa) began landing at Cavalaire and drove north up the Rhône to help free France. The sand you're sunbathing on is a place of remembrance. One real thing: France was liberated from the south as well as the north. Signal Verified: Operation Dragoon landings 15 Aug 1944 (Alpha Beach = Cavalaire, US 3rd Infantry Division); de Lattre's Army B began landing ~7pm on 16 Aug 1944; monument on the Promenade de la Mer — Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur Tourism
